headline: Fragrance-free and unscented are not the same

chunks.text: Shoppers who want to avoid [[fragrance]] may {{watch out for}} two words on a label: "fragrance-free" and "unscented." These words do not mean the same thing. The American Academy of Dermatology says parents of children with [[eczema]] should {{pick out}} fragrance-free products, not unscented ones. Labels may also change. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration plans a rule on fragrance [[allergens]].

verbs.wrong: To print words on a bottle
verbs.why: I always watch out for sugar on food labels. She watches out for sales at her favorite store. Shoppers who want to avoid fragrance may watch out for two words on a label.

verbs.correct: To choose something from a group
verbs.wrong: To decide the price of something
verbs.why: Most shoppers pick out their own fruit at the market. Many parents pick out safe soaps for babies. The academy says parents should pick out fragrance-free products for children with eczema.

chunks.text: Fragrance in [[cosmetics]] is a mix of many natural and [[man-made]] chemicals. The agency says some of them may cause [[allergic reactions]] in some people. Children with eczema have very [[sensitive skin]], and many products can {{set off}} the problem. Their skin may {{break out}} a few hours or even days after a product is used. This can make the cause hard to find. The academy tells parents to {{cut out}} scented shampoo and [[laundry detergent]].

verbs.wrong: To name something on a label
verbs.why: Pollen often sets off sneezing in spring. Cheap perfume sets off headaches for some people. Many products can set off eczema in children with very sensitive skin.

verbs.correct: To suddenly get spots or a rash
verbs.wrong: To be listed as an ingredient
verbs.why: My skin breaks out when I feel stressed. Many teenagers break out before a big event. A child's skin may break out a few hours or even days after a product is used.
Many people cut out sugar to lose weight. Some families cut out soda for a whole year. The academy tells parents of children with eczema to cut out scented shampoo and laundry detergent.

chunks.text: A fragrance-free product should {{leave out}} every ingredient added for its smell. An [[unscented]] product may still contain fragrance. The agency says some makers add just enough to {{cover up}} the [[unpleasant]] smell of other ingredients. A science office at a Canadian university gives an example. If [[lavender]] is hidden in an unscented product, a person who is allergic to it may not {{find out}} that it is there. A fragrance-free product can still smell a little. An oil that softens skin may {{give off}} this light smell.

verbs.wrong: To stack something on a shelf
verbs.why: A good cook leaves out the onions for picky eaters. Short news stories often leave out small details. A fragrance-free product should leave out every ingredient added for its smell.

verbs.correct: To hide something so it is not noticed
verbs.wrong: To list something on the package
verbs.why: A scented candle covers up the smell of cooking fish. Air fresheners only cover up bad smells. Some makers add just enough fragrance to cover up the unpleasant smell of other ingredients.

verbs.correct: To learn a fact you did not know
verbs.wrong: To make a soap smell stronger
verbs.why: Many travelers find out about late flights by text. Shoppers find out store hours on the website. A person who is allergic to lavender may not find out that it is hidden in an unscented product.
Old fish gives off a strong smell. These flowers give off a sweet smell at night. In a fragrance-free product, an oil that softens skin may give off a light smell.

chunks.text: On U.S. [[ingredient lists]], a mix of many scent chemicals can {{show up}} as the single word "fragrance." The agency says the law does not force companies to share these [[trade secrets]]. A 2022 law told it to make a rule on fragrance allergens. A government plan published on July 3, 2026, said the agency expected to [[propose]] the rule in November 2026. The rule would {{spell out}} which allergens must be named on labels.

verbs.wrong: To be priced in a store
verbs.why: Late payments show up on your credit report. Some charges show up twice on a phone bill. On U.S. ingredient lists, many scent chemicals can show up as the single word "fragrance."
Most teachers spell out the rules before a test. A lease spells out how much rent you pay each month. The new rule would spell out which allergens must be named on labels.

ex: Watch out for spelling mistakes when you check your essay.
We watch out for nuts on every menu because of my son's allergy.
Watch out for extra fees when you book a flight.

ex: I break out in a rash if I wear wool.

Some babies break out in a rash in hot weather.

wordDefs.def: A pleasant smell, or something added to give one
ex: This soap has a light fragrance of lemon.
The store sells candles with a strong fragrance.
Some people cannot stand the fragrance of cheap perfume.

wordDefs.def: A skin problem that makes skin red, dry and itchy
ex: My little brother has eczema on his hands.
Cold, dry weather can make eczema worse.
She uses a thick cream for her eczema.

wordDefs.def: Things that can cause an allergic reaction
ex: Peanuts and milk are common allergens.
Dust and pet hair are allergens for many people.
The menu lists the main allergens in each dish.

wordDefs.def: Products such as makeup, lotion and shampoo that people put on their body
ex: She keeps her cosmetics in a small bag.
That store sells cosmetics and perfume.
Many cosmetics are tested before they are sold.

wordDefs.def: Made by people, not found in nature
ex: The park has a small man-made lake.
Nylon is a man-made material.
Some man-made scents smell like real flowers.

wordDefs.def: Bad effects on the body caused by something a person cannot handle
ex: Some people have allergic reactions to peanuts.
Bee stings can cause serious allergic reactions.
The nurse asked if I had any allergic reactions to medicine.

wordDefs.def: Skin that easily gets red, dry or sore
ex: People with sensitive skin should test a new cream on a small spot first.
This soap is made for babies with sensitive skin.
My sensitive skin gets red in the cold wind.
We ran out of laundry detergent, so I went to the store.
Use only a little laundry detergent in this machine.
This laundry detergent comes in a big blue bottle.

wordDefs.def: Made to have no smell that you can notice
ex: She buys unscented lotion because perfume gives her headaches.
The hotel uses unscented soap in every room.
Unscented candles are popular in restaurants.

wordDefs.def: A plant with small purple flowers and a strong smell
ex: My grandmother grows lavender in her garden.

wordDefs.def: Lists on a package that name what a product contains
ex: I always read ingredient lists when I buy bread.
Some ingredient lists are very long and hard to read.
Ingredient lists name the biggest part of the product first.

wordDefs.def: Information a company keeps private so others cannot copy it
ex: The recipe for the sauce is one of the restaurant's trade secrets.
Workers must promise not to share trade secrets.
The company sued a rival for stealing its trade secrets.

wordDefs.def: To officially suggest a plan or rule
ex: The city wants to propose a new bus route.
She will propose a shorter workweek at the meeting.
Lawmakers plan to propose a new tax next year.

mainIdea.s: Fragrance-free and unscented labels do not mean the same thing, because an unscented product can still hold hidden fragrance. U.S. officials also plan a rule on fragrance allergens.
mainIdea.why: Skin doctors say parents should pick out fragrance-free products. Unscented ones may hide fragrance, and the agency plans a rule to spell out which allergens labels must name.

mainIdea.s: Unscented goods are just as safe as fragrance-free ones, so skin doctors say either kind works for kids with eczema. A new rule would make every scent chemical appear on labels.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the two labels do not mean the same thing. Skin doctors say parents should pick out fragrance-free products, and the rule is about allergens, not every chemical.

mainIdea.s: A new law in the U.S. bans perfume and scented soap in public schools and hospitals. Officials say the ban starts next spring after many complaints from parents, teachers and nurses.
mainIdea.why: There is no such ban. Fragrance-free and unscented labels differ, and the agency plans a rule to spell out which allergens labels must name.

tf.s: Skin doctors say parents should pick out fragrance-free products for children with eczema.
tf.why: The academy says parents should choose fragrance-free products rather than unscented ones.

tf.s: The words fragrance-free and unscented mean the same thing.
tf.why: They do not mean the same thing. A fragrance-free product should leave out every ingredient added for its smell.

tf.s: Some makers add fragrance to cover up the smell of other ingredients.
tf.why: This is why a product labeled "unscented" may still contain fragrance.

tf.s: An unscented product never contains any fragrance.
tf.why: A person allergic to lavender may not find out that it is hidden in an unscented product.

tf.s: The planned rule would stop labels from naming any fragrance allergens.
tf.why: The rule would spell out which fragrance allergens must be named on labels.

tf.s: Many scent chemicals can show up on a label as just one word.
tf.why: Companies do not have to share these trade secrets, so the full mix is not listed.

lines.text: I always buy unscented soap. That's better for my skin, right?
Not always. Unscented and fragrance-free aren't the same thing.
Wait, really? I thought they meant the same.
An unscented product can still have fragrance. Some makers add a little to {{cover up}} the smell of other ingredients.
Well, [[I stand corrected]]. So which one should I buy?
Fragrance-free. Always {{watch out for}} that word on the label. Skin doctors tell parents of kids with eczema to {{pick out}} fragrance-free products.
Why does it matter so much?
Some ingredients can {{set off}} a reaction. And your skin might {{break out}} days later.
So it's hard to know what caused it.
Exactly. And a long list of scent chemicals can {{show up}} on the label as just one word.
So reading labels is [[hit or miss]].
For now. The government plans a rule to {{spell out}} which allergens labels must name.
Good. With skin problems, [[you can't be too careful]].
True. Even a fragrance-free cream can smell a little. An oil that softens skin can {{give off}} that smell.
Well, [[live and learn]]. I'm buying fragrance-free from now on.

expressions.def: Used to admit that you were wrong about something
ex: I thought the store opened at nine, but I stand corrected.
You're right, it was Tuesday. I stand corrected.

expressions.def: Used to say that something is good sometimes and bad other times
ex: The food at that cafe is hit or miss.
Buying shoes online can be hit or miss.

expressions.def: Used to say that it is wise to be very careful
ex: Lock the car, even here. You can't be too careful.

expressions.def: Used to say that you learned something from a mistake
ex: I paid too much for that phone. Oh well, live and learn.

expressions.def: Used to say that someone made a smart choice
ex: You brought an umbrella? Good call.
Good call on leaving early. The traffic is terrible.
